title: Standards and Specification Guidelines for Use Cases & Software Requirements Engineering

slides.title: From Product Description to Use Cases
bullets: Unstructured product descriptions are the starting point
Standards give a shared vocabulary
Spec‑driven development turns descriptions into executable specs
slides.notes: Open the lecture by framing the problem: we receive a narrative product description and must produce precise use cases. Standards provide the common language that lets analysts, developers, and testers agree on what the system must do. Spec‑driven development then uses those use cases as executable specifications that can drive code generation and test creation.

slides.title: Why Use‑Case Standards Matter
bullets: Common language for stakeholders
Enables traceability to code and tests
Supports tooling and automation
slides.notes: Without a standard notation, each team invents its own way of writing use cases, leading to ambiguity and gaps. A shared standard lets requirements be traced forward to design, code, and test cases, and it enables tools to parse, validate, and even generate artifacts automatically.

slides.title: Key Use‑Case Standards: UML 2.x & OMG Template
bullets: UML 2.x defines use‑case diagram notation
OMG provides a textual use‑case template
Both are maintained by the Object Management Group

figure.caption: Core elements of a UML use‑case diagram

slides.notes: UML 2.x is the de‑facto graphical standard for use‑case diagrams; the OMG also publishes a textual template (often called the Cockburn template) that captures preconditions, postconditions, main flow, and alternatives. Both are actively maintained and widely supported by modeling tools.

slides.title: Requirements Specification Standard: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
bullets: Replaces withdrawn IEEE 830 (2017)
Structures SRS: purpose, scope, functional & non‑functional requirements
Guides traceability and verification
slides.notes: IEEE 830 was withdrawn in 2017. The current international standard for writing Software Requirements Specifications is ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, which defines the required sections of an SRS and emphasizes bidirectional traceability between requirements, design, and test.

slides.title: Quality Model: ISO/IEC 25010
bullets: Defines product quality characteristics (e.g., functionality, reliability)
Not a use‑case standard but informs non‑functional requirements
Used to derive quality‑focused use cases
slides.notes: ISO/IEC 25010 (2018 edition) provides a taxonomy of quality attributes such as performance, security, and usability. While it does not define use‑case notation, it is the reference for writing non‑functional requirements that later become quality‑focused use cases or acceptance criteria.

slides.title: Example: Online Ordering Use‑Case Diagram
bullets: Actors: Customer, Payment Service, Inventory Service
Use cases: Place Order, Process Payment, Check Inventory
Include relationships: Place Order includes Process Payment and Check Inventory

figure.caption: Simplified flow for the Place Order use case

slides.notes: Walk through the diagram: the Customer initiates Place Order. The system includes two sub‑use cases — Process Payment (interacting with the external Payment Service actor) and Check Inventory (interacting with the Inventory Service actor). Both are marked with «include» because they are mandatory parts of every order.

slides.title: Identifying the System Boundary
bullets: Boundary encloses responsibilities of the system under design
Actors and external systems stay outside
Clarifies scope for development and testing
slides.notes: The system boundary is a conceptual line that separates what the project team must build from what is given (actors, external services, hardware). It is drawn on the use‑case diagram as a rectangle; everything inside is in scope, everything outside is an actor or an external system.

slides.title: Example: System Boundary for Mobile Banking App
bullets: Actors: Customer, Bank Server, Regulator
Inside boundary: Mobile App UI, Local Validation, Transaction Logic
Outside: Bank Server APIs, Regulatory Reporting Service

figure.caption: Actors and the mobile‑app system boundary

slides.notes: Choose a single coherent scope — here the mobile client. The Customer interacts with the app; the app calls Bank Server APIs (outside) for core banking functions; the Regulator receives compliance reports via a separate reporting service (also outside). This makes clear which components the team must deliver.

slides.title: Spec‑Driven Development Guidelines for Use Cases
bullets: Write use cases as executable specifications
Link each use case to acceptance criteria
Generate test scaffolding from use‑case steps
slides.notes: Spec‑driven development treats a well‑structured use case (with clear preconditions, main flow, and postconditions) as a living specification. Tools can parse the steps to generate BDD‑style test skeletons, API contracts, or even prototype code, keeping implementation aligned with requirements.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Extract Use Cases from a Short Product Description
bullets: Step 1: Identify actors from nouns
Step 2: List user goals as use cases
Step 3: Draw system boundary
Step 4: Add include/extend relationships
Step 5: Write brief textual template for each use case
slides.notes: Given a paragraph describing a ‘library self‑checkout’ system, we first spot actors (Patron, Librarian, Catalog Service). Next we write goals: ‘Check out book’, ‘Return book’, ‘Pay fine’. We draw a boundary around the self‑checkout kiosk software, add «include» for ‘Authenticate Patron’ used by both check‑out and return, and finally fill the OMG textual template for each use case.

slides.title: Check: Use‑Case Identification

quiz.question: Which artifact is defined by UML 2.x for visualizing use cases?
quiz.explanation: UML 2.x defines the use‑case diagram notation; class, sequence, and state machine diagrams serve other purposes.

slides.notes: Common confusion: class diagram shows structure, not use cases. The use‑case diagram is the only UML diagram whose primary purpose is to capture functional requirements from the user's perspective.

slides.title: Software Requirements Engineering Overview
bullets: Elicitation, analysis, specification, validation, management
Iterative and incremental in modern practice
Bridges stakeholder needs and technical solution
slides.notes: Requirements engineering is the disciplined process of discovering, documenting, and maintaining what the software must do. It is not a one‑shot activity; modern projects revisit each phase as knowledge grows.

slides.title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques
bullets: Interviews and workshops
Observation and ethnography
Prototyping and storyboarding
slides.notes: No single technique suffices. Interviews uncover detailed needs, workshops align stakeholders, and prototypes make abstract ideas concrete. Combining them reduces the risk of missing critical requirements.

slides.title: Requirements Analysis & Modeling
bullets: Use cases and user stories capture functional needs
Domain models clarify data concepts
Non‑functional requirements mapped to ISO/IEC 25010
slides.notes: Analysis transforms raw elicitation data into structured models. Use cases (or user stories) describe behavior; domain models (class diagrams, ER diagrams) capture data; quality attributes from ISO/IEC 25010 become non‑functional requirements with measurable targets.

slides.title: Requirements Specification & Validation
bullets: SRS structured per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
Reviews, inspections, and prototypes validate completeness
Traceability matrix links requirements to tests
slides.notes: The SRS is the contract between stakeholders and developers. Following ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 ensures all required sections exist. Validation uses peer reviews, executable prototypes, and a traceability matrix to confirm every requirement is testable and covered.

slides.title: Requirements Management & Traceability
bullets: Version control for requirements artifacts
Change impact analysis via trace links
Tool support (e.g., DOORS, Jama, Git‑based)
slides.notes: Requirements evolve. A management process stores each version, records rationale, and maintains trace links to design, code, and tests. When a requirement changes, impact analysis shows which downstream artifacts must be updated. Modern tools integrate with Git to keep requirements close to the codebase.

slides.title: Check: Requirements Engineering Activities

quiz.question: Which standard structures a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) today?
quiz.explanation: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 superseded IEEE 830 in 2017; ISO/IEC 25010 is a quality model, and UML 2.x defines diagrams, not SRS structure.

slides.notes: Remember IEEE 830 is withdrawn. The current SRS standard is ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, which also emphasizes traceability and verification.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: UML 2.x & OMG template standardize use‑case notation
ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 guides SRS structure
ISO/IEC 25010 informs quality requirements
System boundary defines scope of the system under design
Spec‑driven development turns use cases into executable specs
Requirements engineering cycles through elicitation, analysis, specification, validation, management
slides.notes: Recap the main points: use‑case standards give a common language, the SRS standard structures the full specification, the quality model shapes non‑functional needs, and the system boundary sets scope. Spec‑driven development leverages these artifacts for automation. The requirements engineering lifecycle ties everything together and prepares us for next week’s spec‑driven frameworks.
